wa_cascade_peak_east_ridge.name: Up the Cascade-Johannesburg Couloir to the C-J col
wa_cascade_peak_east_ridge.notes:
The East Ridge is reached from the Cascade-Johannesburg col, and the direct way there is to climb the couloir that names it. The start is the Cascade Pass trailhead at about 3,600 ft: walk back down the road, drop the embankment into the valley, cross the Cascade River, and go over the moraine onto the couloir apron at roughly 3,300 ft — about twenty minutes from leaving the road. Then roughly 3,400 ft of booting to the col.

This is the fast way and the dangerous way. The couloir carries rock and ice fall from the Sill hanging glacier above, and the snow goes discontinuous where it narrows as the season progresses, so it is an early-season proposition.

The East Ridge by way of the C-J Couloir was first climbed in 1938 and is the most-used line on the peak; it and the other routes finishing on the south side are mostly scrambling.
wa_cascade_peak_east_ridge.season: May-Jun for continuous snow in the couloir
hazards: Rock and ice fall from the Sill hanging glacier in the couloir
Discontinuous couloir snow after early season
Loose rock and complicated route-finding on the ridge above the col
Existing rappel stations of unknown quality
wa_cascade_peak_east_ridge.baseFinding:
The base of the climbing is the Cascade-Johannesburg col itself — the notch at the top of the couloir, with Johannesburg on one side and Cascade Peak on the other. There is no ambiguity about arriving: the snow ends against the saddle and the ground drops away on the far side.

From the col the East Ridge is the crest running west toward Cascade Peak's summit, on your right as you top out of the couloir. Published descriptions of the ground above are thin and consistent on one point only: route-finding is complicated, exposure is significant, and loose rock is everywhere. Parties commonly climb it unroped while carrying a harness in case they want a belay.

There are numerous rappel stations scattered around this area from previous parties, and reports note that some of them need improving before use — treat a found anchor as information, not as confirmation you are on route.

wa_cascade_peak_east_ridge.name: Cascade Pass, Mixup Arm and the Cache Glacier
wa_cascade_peak_east_ridge.notes:
The walking way in, avoiding the couloir entirely. Follow the Cascade Pass Trail from the trailhead at 3,600 ft for 3.5-3.7 miles and about 1,800 ft to Cascade Pass at roughly 5,400 ft. At the pass, near the benches, turn right and pick up the obvious climbers' path onto Mixup Arm.

Cross Mixup Arm and traverse and descend rightward until you reach the Cache Glacier — the described landmark is a seasonal waterfall, past which you turn right and ascend the lobe of the Cache.

One party using this side reported a long sidehill traverse beneath the Triplets and Cascade Peak, camping in a meadow below the C-J col at about 6,200 ft. That camp puts you at the base of the East Ridge for the following morning without ever entering the couloir.

Early season the traverse across Mixup's flank is snow-covered with a poor runout; late season Cache Col and the glacier edges can moat out.
hazards: Snow-covered traverse on Mixup's flank with bad runout in early season
Cache Col and glacier margins moat out late season
Steep short snow tongue and flanking bergschrunds at Gunsight Notch
Rockfall in the confined ground between snow and rock at the notch
wa_cascade_peak_east_ridge.baseFinding:
Approaching from this side you arrive at the C-J col or the meadows just below it rather than climbing up to it, so the confirmation is positional: the col is the saddle between Johannesburg and Cascade Peak at the head of the couloir, and from the meadow camp below it the East Ridge runs up on the Cascade Peak side.

Gunsight Notch — the prominent notch to the west of Cache Col — is the published portal from the Cache Glacier side for Mix-Up, the Triplets and Cascade Peak, so a party approaching Cascade Peak from the Cache rather than from the col is aiming at that notch instead. The snow tongue to Gunsight Notch is short, about a hundred feet, but steep at roughly 50-65 degrees, with bergschrunds on either side of it dropping ten to fifteen feet to a rock floor, and rockfall in tight quarters between snow and rock.

wa_castle_peak_pasayten_scramble.name: Ross Lake boat crossing, Lightning Creek trail and the abandoned Freezeout Creek trail
wa_castle_peak_pasayten_scramble.notes:
This is the way in that stays entirely inside the United States, and it is the reason the peak costs three or four days.

From the highway pullout above the dam, a short spur trail drops to the lake shore. Cross the lake by water taxi, or paddle a private or inflatable boat portaged down that spur, and land near the head of the lake where the Lightning Creek trail starts at about 1,500 ft. Parties with their own boat commonly start walking around four in the morning to leave daylight for the day above; the water taxi runs only in the daytime, 8am to 5pm.

After a couple of hours watch for the junction with the old, no-longer-maintained Freezeout Creek trail. The stretch immediately above that junction is the hardest navigation of the entire approach: steep rock and alder slopes that want a rising, diagonal line before you regain forest and real tread. Intermittent orange flagging marks it and is worth hunting for.

Back in the trees the tread improves up to a cabin at about 3,600 ft, sited just after a creek crossing — bunks, a wood stove and a logbook, and a useful emergency shelter. About a quarter mile past it, cross the creek again and pass through an old burn. Tread mostly disappears around 4,200 ft.

The lower part of this corridor is national recreation area and needs a park backcountry permit for camping; above the boundary it is wilderness with a free self-issue permit.
wa_castle_peak_pasayten_scramble.season: Late July through September in a normal year; the creek is hard to ford until the snowmelt drops
hazards: Abandoned Freezeout Creek trail with heavy blowdown, brush and a hard rock-and-alder diagonal above the junction
Freezeout Creek crossings can be high and hazardous early season
Several similar gullies in the upper basin; the wrong one cliffs out above the creek
Loose talus and teetering blocks near the summit; lingering snow patches early season
Boat crossing of Ross Lake with a limited-hours water taxi; long days often finish the descent in the dark
Bear country, no cell coverage, multi-day retreat
wa_castle_peak_pasayten_scramble.baseFinding:
There is no rock start to find on this route. What you are finding is the right gully out of a basin that offers several, and getting that wrong is how parties get cliffed out.

Above where the tread dies, climb the Freezeout drainage and work up steep heather, talus and scree toward the notch on the ridge at about 7,600 ft. That notch is the target and it is the only feature in the upper basin worth navigating to. Cross to the east side of the creek at roughly 5,000 ft on the way up.

The physical tests on the climb itself are rock quality and terrain grade, in that order. This is granite and the rock is genuinely good — clean, coarse and solid, the sort people compare to the best cragging ranges. It is mostly class 2 with short class 3 steps, and the crux is a steeper band with krummholz and bluffs where you are pulling on vegetation-covered rock. If you are roping up, you are off route.

The negative marker is enormous and unmistakable. This peak's north side is a fourteen-hundred-foot wall of granite ribs, gullies and couloirs holding ice or the remains of it, with a glacier at its foot. If you are looking up at that, you are on the wrong side of the mountain entirely and you are under the technical routes. The scramble never sees the north face.

Mark your exact ascent gully before you leave it, and this is the single most important sentence here. The upper basin holds several gullies and chutes that look alike from above, and dropping into the wrong one on descent risks cliffing out on bluffs well above the creek. Do not improvise a shortcut down. Reverse exactly what you came up.

Near the summit, watch teetering blocks, and expect the final ground to be exposed and windy.

wa_castle_peak_pasayten_scramble.name: The crest trail north from Harts Pass to Castle Pass
wa_castle_peak_pasayten_scramble.notes:
The third way in, and the one that trades a boat for a great deal of walking. The high pass road climbs roughly twenty miles of unpaved single lane from Mazama with pullouts rather than passing room, a rock wall on one side and an unguarded drop on the other, and grades approaching seventeen percent on the upper ramps. Trailers are prohibited and wide vehicles are strongly discouraged. It opens with the snowmelt, typically early to mid July, and closes with the first serious autumn storms.

From the pass, the crest trail runs north through country that starts near 6,200 ft and barely drops below 5,000 ft, over a high pass and on to Castle Pass, where it meets the Boundary Trail running east across the Pasayten and west toward the lake. Camps along the way are open and windy; pitch behind timber rather than in the meadow.

This stays inside the United States throughout, and it needs no boat.
wa_castle_peak_pasayten_scramble.season: Late July through September, once the high road is open and the traverse is clear of snow
hazards: Long unpaved mountain road, steep grades, no passing room, unguarded drop; opens late and closes with early storms
Very long walk in with exposed, windy high camps
The international boundary is about a mile north of the summit; crossing it here is unlawful
Similar-looking descent gullies that cliff out above the creek
Loose talus and teetering blocks near the summit; lingering snow patches early season
Bear country, no cell coverage, multi-day retreat
wa_castle_peak_pasayten_scramble.baseFinding:
From Castle Pass the peak lies roughly four miles to the west-northwest, and what you are looking for is the head of the drainage on its southern flank rather than a base of rock.

Drop off the pass into the head of the creek basin on the peak's south side and work up it. The scramble ground is the same ground the eastern approach reaches from the other direction: heather, talus and scree leading to the notch on the ridge at about 7,600 ft, then class 2 granite with short class 3 steps to the summit.

The confirming test is the rock. Once you are on it, the granite is clean, coarse and solid, and the difficulty stays at scrambling grade with one steeper krummholz-and-bluff band as the crux. Roped climbing means you are not on the standard route.

Negative marker, and it is the whole mountain: the north side is a fourteen-hundred-foot granite wall above a glacier. From anywhere on this approach you should be looking at broken scrambling ground, not at a wall. If a wall is above you, you have gone round the mountain.

Second negative marker, and it is a legal one rather than a navigational one. The summit sits about a mile south of the international boundary and the boundary clearing is visible from high on the peak. Do not follow ground north from the summit or from the basin. Crossing on foot away from a port of entry is not a lawful crossing, the corridor is patrolled, and this is the one mistake here that ends with more than a long walk.

On descent, mark your ascent gully. The basin holds several that look alike from above and the wrong one cliffs out.

wa_castle_peak_pasayten_the_drawbridge.name: Ross Lake boat crossing, Lightning Creek and the abandoned Freezeout Creek trail to the north-face glacier
wa_castle_peak_pasayten_the_drawbridge.notes:
This is the approach that stays inside the United States, and it is a multi-day trudge rather than a walk.

From the highway pullout above the dam a short spur trail drops to the lake shore. Cross by water taxi or by a boat you portage down that spur, and land near the head of the lake where the Lightning Creek trail begins. Follow it, then pick up the abandoned and increasingly brushy Freezeout Creek trail, whose worst navigation is the steep rock-and-alder diagonal immediately above the junction — intermittent orange flagging marks it. The cabin at about 3,600 ft is a good waypoint and an emergency shelter; tread mostly dies around 4,200 ft.

The lower corridor is national recreation area and camping there needs a park backcountry permit; the upper part is wilderness with a free self-issue permit.

From the upper basin, cross round to the north side and onto the glacier at the foot of the wall. The glacier itself is mellow and allows easy travel.
wa_castle_peak_pasayten_the_drawbridge.season: Roughly late June through September, once the approach glacier and moraine are passable
hazards: Multi-day approach by boat and abandoned, brushy trail; steep rock-and-alder diagonal above the junction
Several unmarked routes on a 1,400 ft wall; identification is by position under the summit only
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the start of the climbing
Rockfall on the lower wall, worst once sun hits the face
Dirt- and moss-filled cracks mid-route and teetering blocks near the top
No cell coverage and an extremely slow retreat
wa_castle_peak_pasayten_the_drawbridge.baseFinding:
The north face is a wall of granite ribs, gullies and couloirs about fourteen hundred feet high, holding ice or the remnants of it, with a glacier at its foot. It carries several routes and they are not marked, so identification is by position against the summit and nothing else.

The test is simple and it is the whole identification: this route takes the central buttress, and that buttress sits directly below the summit. Stand back on the glacier, find the summit on the skyline, and drop a plumb line from it. The buttress under that line is this route. If the summit is off to one side from where you are standing, you are under a different climb.

Getting onto it is the second problem. Expect an awkward bergschrund or moat where the glacier meets the rock, and start with easy fifth-class ground whose purpose is to get out of the rockfall line rather than to climb anything — that first pitch is a position move, not a feature.

Confirm on pitch two, because it arrives fast and it is unmistakable: the crux comes almost immediately, mid-fifth-class face climbing hard enough that the first ascent used a short aid move to pass it. A wall this size whose hardest pitch is the second one is unusual, and it is the strongest evidence you are on line.

The middle of the route then traverses out of a dihedral on a tricky flake and takes a roof on the left via cracks and stemming, over slabs that needed heavy cleaning of dirt and moss. After about five pitches the route gains the ridge proper and the rock quality improves markedly, with one short harder hand-and-fist crack. The final technical pitch picks its way around teetering blocks, and then moderate snow slopes run the last four hundred feet to the top.

Negative marker: if your line starts in a blocky set of face holds beside a gully or chimney at the left edge of the buttress, you are on the neighbouring route at the buttress's left margin, and higher up it follows a distinctive yellow quartz dyke that this route does not touch.

Descent is not the climb reversed. Walk off the south side and the east ridge back toward camp.

wa_castle_peak_pasayten_the_drawbridge.name: Provincial park approach from the north over Frosty Mountain to Crow Creek

approachLogistics.trailhead: Lightning Lake, E.C. Manning Provincial Park (British Columbia)

wa_castle_peak_pasayten_the_drawbridge.notes:
Read the legal point first. This line walks in from the provincial park on the northern side and then crosses the international boundary cross-country. That is not a lawful crossing. Away from a port of entry it requires prior arrangement with the border authority, the corridor is patrolled, and casual parties cannot simply walk over. It is the first-ascent line, not a recommendation.

It starts from the lake in the provincial park, climbs up and over Frosty Mountain, descends into the next creek basin to the south, traverses to the divide, and drops into the Crow Creek drainage below the peak's north face. The first ascent camped on the only dry spot on the ridge, roughly two-thirds of the way down toward the glacier.

The wholly lawful alternatives are the boat crossing and abandoned creek trail from the east, or the crest trail from the west.
hazards: The described line crosses the international boundary cross-country, which is not a lawful crossing
Cross-country travel over a mountain and two drainage divides, one dry camp on the ridge
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the base of the wall
Rockfall on the lower face; loose blocks near the top of the technical climbing
Retreat from anywhere on the trip is measured in days
wa_castle_peak_pasayten_the_drawbridge.baseFinding:
However you reach it, the glacier at the foot of the wall is the same and the identification is the same.

Come down the ridge from camp to the glacier, which is mellow enough to walk. Then stand back far enough to see the whole face at once — this is the step the approach itself makes easy from this side, because you descend toward the wall rather than arriving under it, and a descending approach gives you the one view that settles the route.

From that view, drop a plumb line from the summit. The buttress under it is this route. The face carries several other lines and none is marked; being under the summit is the identification.

Watch for an awkward bergschrund or moat where the glacier meets the rock. The first pitch is easy fifth-class ground taken to escape the rockfall line rather than for the climbing, and the crux arrives at once on pitch two — face climbing hard enough that a short aid move was used on the first ascent.

Negative marker: a start in blocky face holds beside a gully or chimney at the left edge of the buttress is the neighbouring route, which follows a yellow quartz dyke higher up.

Second negative marker, and it applies from the moment you leave camp: the boundary clearing is a visible cut line on this ground and it is not a route. The summit sits about a mile south of it.

Descent is the south side and the east ridge, unroped third and fourth-class ground from the top of the technical climbing, back toward camp.

wa_castle_peak_pasayten_the_drawbridge.name: Pacific Crest Trail north from Harts Pass
wa_castle_peak_pasayten_the_drawbridge.notes: Follow the Pacific Crest Trail north from Harts Pass along the crest, about 27 miles to Castle Pass, then go cross-country onto the peak and around to the north side. It needs no boat and stays in the United States, but it is a very long high walk and the Harts Pass road usually opens only in July.
hazards: About 27 miles of high walking on the crest to Castle Pass before any off-trail travel
Harts Pass road usually opens only in July
Cross-country onto the peak and around to the north side, then the glacier at the wall's foot
Rockfall on the lower wall and loose blocks near the top of the technical climbing
Awkward bergschrund or moat; no cell coverage and a multi-day retreat

wa_cathedral_peak_last_rites.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 from the Chewuch River road
wa_cathedral_peak_last_rites.notes:
Drive north from Winthrop up the Chewuch River road to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,050 ft. This is the shortest drive of the three ways in and it is paved the whole way.

Walk Andrews Creek trail #504 up the drainage. The lower miles cross an old burn, so there is almost no shade, the tread is overgrown and soaks you after rain, and blowdown is normal. Andrews Creek runs beside the trail for that whole stretch and is reliable water. The trail tops out at Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft, where the burn gives way to open parkland.

From the pass continue on the Boundary Trail #533 and drop on the Cathedral Lakes side trail to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft. Bear off near the old wilderness guard-station cabin. Strong parties walk it in one long day with heavy packs; others split it with a camp partway up the drainage.

One thing to leave alone: there is a shorter-looking way in from the Canadian side. Crossing into the United States here is illegal, the border is patrolled, and the penalties are severe.
wa_cathedral_peak_last_rites.season: Roughly mid-July through September, once the trails and the face have shed snow
hazards: Rockfall from parties above and from loose blocks on the featured face; helmets from the base
Old burn on Andrews Creek: no shade, overgrown wet tread, blowdown
No climbers' trail to the base; identify it by landform
Afternoon storms and lightning on the local high point
Early- and shoulder-season snow and verglas on the upper face and summit chasm
Walk-off crux is a no-fall step across a gap near the summit
No cell coverage and a 17+ mile trail evacuation; wildfire smoke and closures late summer
wa_cathedral_peak_last_rites.baseFinding:
There is no climbers' trail to the base. Cross the parkland and talus from camp toward the deep gully that divides Cathedral Peak from The Monk, the semi-detached tower leaning against the lower right side of the wall. Thirty to sixty minutes from camp.

The first test is the tower, and it is a negative one. This route is on the main wall, not on the tower and not on the buttress behind it. If a separate tower stands between you and the rock you are about to climb, walk further left along the base — you are under the Southeast Buttress. If you are looking up at an open thousand-foot face with nothing standing in front of it, you are in the right place.

Now place yourself across that face. This line takes the right-hand portion of the open wall, between the central line and the line further right. There is no start ledge, no cairn and no fixed gear to find; the ground low down is heavily featured and the first ascent treated it as choose-your-own, so the start is a zone rather than a point. Pick the most featured rock in that right-hand third and go up.

Confirm it above you before you commit, because the low ground will accept almost any line. Look for a long ramp slashing rightward across the middle of the face, and above the ramp a steep, clean crack splitting a headwall. Those two features in that order are this route. If the ramp is not there and instead you find a big curving chimney above you, you have drifted into the centre of the wall and you are on the original central line — several number grades easier, and a different day.

Second negative marker, at the top: this route joins the buttress route for its final hand crack to the summit. Arriving at that shared pitch is correct. Arriving at it early, without having crossed a rightward ramp and pulled a thin headwall, means you traversed off.

wa_cathedral_peak_last_rites.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee
wa_cathedral_peak_last_rites.notes:
This is a trail, #510A, not a four-wheel-drive road, despite a persistent claim to the contrary — the high-clearance warning in circulation belongs to a different spur road. Access is from Loomis by Toats Coulee Road, then a Y junction, then the forest roads up to the trailhead at about 5,570 ft.

Be careful with the trailhead name. It appears in print under three or four spellings, and one of those names also belongs to a completely different trailhead near Winthrop. Navigate to the road, not to the name.

The trail descends from its high trailhead to join the valley trail below, and from there it is the valley to the Cathedral Lakes basin. This is the shortest walk and the least climbing of the ways in.

The catch sits at both ends. The drive is about two hours longer than from Winthrop, and because the trailhead is high and the trail drops to meet the valley, you finish the trip with roughly 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out, at the point when you least want it.
hazards: 1,300 ft of climbing at the very end of the trip on the way out
Trailhead published under several names, one shared with a different trailhead; navigate to the road
No climbers' trail to the base
Rockfall from parties above and loose blocks on the face
Afternoon storms and lightning; snow and verglas on the upper face early or late season
Walk-off crux is a no-fall step across a gap near the summit
No cell coverage and a long trail evacuation
wa_cathedral_peak_last_rites.baseFinding:
The way in changes; the base does not. From Upper Cathedral Lake it is the same walk toward the deep gully dividing Cathedral Peak from The Monk, and the same question at the bottom: is there a tower standing between you and the rock? If yes you are under the buttress, not this face.

What this approach genuinely changes is your first sighting of the wall. Coming up the valley you arrive in the basin from below rather than over the pass, so the whole south side presents itself at once from across the water. Use that. Standing at the lake, pick out three things before you walk up: the tower at the lower right of the wall, the open thousand-foot face left of it, and the long ramp that slashes rightward across the middle of that face. This route is the right-hand third of the open face, working up to that ramp and to the steep crack in the headwall above it.

That identification is far easier from across the lake than from underneath, where the face foreshortens and the ramp disappears into the general featuring. Photograph it or draw it before you leave camp.

Negative marker: if from the lake you cannot see a ramp at all on the face you are looking at, you are looking at the wrong wall. The tower has its own south face with its own short routes on it, and beta written about that tower will also say South Face. The tower is small and stands clear of the mountain; the main face runs the full height of the peak behind it.

wa_cathedral_peak_last_rites.name: Thirtymile Trailhead and the Chewuch River trail toward Remmel Lake

approachLogistics.trailhead: Thirtymile Trailhead (end of the Chewuch River Road)

wa_cathedral_peak_last_rites.notes: Follow the Chewuch River trail north from the Thirtymile Trailhead nearly to Remmel Lake, then climb to the Cathedral Lakes basin. A longer way round than Andrews Creek, used when combining the Remmel Lake country with the climb.
hazards: Long valley approach on the Chewuch trail, longer than Andrews Creek
No climbers' trail to the base; identify it by landform
Rockfall from parties above and loose blocks on the face
Afternoon storms and lightning; snow and verglas on the upper face early or late season
Walk-off crux is a no-fall step across a gap near the summit
No cell coverage and a long trail evacuation

wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 from the Chewuch River road
camps: Cathedral Pass benches and the tarn slabs
wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.notes:
Drive north from Winthrop up the Chewuch River road to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,080 ft, roughly a five-hour drive from Seattle and the shortest drive of the three ways in.

Walk Andrews Creek trail #504 up the drainage. The lower miles pass through an old burn, so there is little shade and the tread can be overgrown and wet after rain, but the creek is beside you and reliable. The trail tops out at Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft, where the burn gives way to open parkland.

Continue on the Boundary Trail #533 and drop on the Cathedral Lakes side trail to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft. Published figures for the whole walk from this trailhead are about nineteen miles with 5,550 ft of gain, and everyone splits it over at least two days.

Of the three trailheads this one has the shortest drive and the most walking gain; the Thirtymile trailhead is only about five and a half miles further along the same road, which makes a car shuttle between them easy.

One thing to leave alone: there is a shorter-looking approach from the Canadian side. Crossing into the United States here is illegal, the border is patrolled, and the fines are severe.
wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; snow lingers at Andrews Pass into early July
hazards: Long approach through an old burn: little shade, overgrown wet tread
No climbers' trail to the base; navigate by the gully dividing the peak from the tower
Exposed roped climbing; loose, grainy rock on P1 and upper pitches
Hanging belay between P8 and P9 if not linked
No-fall step-across on the walk-off descent
Afternoon thunderstorms; remote, so retreat is slow
Shorter-looking Canadian approach is an illegal border crossing and patrolled
wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.baseFinding: There is no climbers' trail to the base. A party who got there reported finding none and navigating purely off photographs, so stop looking for tread and navigate by the landform. The landform is the deep gully that separates Cathedral Peak from The Monk, the semi-detached tower on the lower right side of the south face. One published account leaves the maintained trail at the first switchback after Cathedral Pass and heads for the gully from there; others come across the parkland between Upper Cathedral Lake and the pass. Both end up in the same place, thirty to sixty minutes from camp. Go up into the gully — do not stop at its mouth. Three accounts put the start of the first pitch about 150 feet up the Cathedral–Monk gully, on the left wall, which is the Cathedral side. Scramble onto a tall pedestal there; it gives a decent belay stance to start from. Pedestal, left wall, about 150 feet in: that is the whole identification. How to tell this from the South Face routes, and it is a simple physical test: is there a semi-detached tower standing between you and the wall? If yes, you are at the SE Buttress, which follows the ridge behind The Monk on the right-hand edge of the south face. If you are walking up to an open face with nothing in front of it, that is the South Face route, a different and much harder climb. A related trap in the naming rather than on the ground: The Monk has its own south face with its own routes on it. Beta headed South Face may be describing the tower, not the mountain. Coming down, the descent is the walk-off to the west and then south-west back toward Upper Cathedral Lake, and its crux is a gap the route description tells you to hop across. It can be avoided by downclimbing the exposed nose beside it and stepping over — easy when dry, but no-fall ground.

wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee

bivy.name: Upper Cathedral Lake basin
bivy.notes: The working climbers' camp for both the Southeast Buttress and Amphitheater's ridges, sitting directly under the peaks with short walks to either. The basin has taken heavy use for decades and the Forest Service has posted revegetation closures on damaged ground here in the past, so treat the shoreline as off limits and camp on rock or bare dirt well back from the water. Check the posted signs on arrival rather than assuming last year's layout still applies — which sites are open has changed between seasons. Nights are cold and exposed at this elevation even in August.
bivy.water: The most dependable water anywhere on this approach — the lake holds through the season and needs no rationing. The one place on the route where you can plan on filling without checking a report first.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at the Andrews Creek trailhead. No quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day fee to park.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites on slabs and benches back from the water; realistically three or four small parties before it feels crowded, and it does fill on midsummer weekends and during larch season

wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.notes:
This is a trail, #510A, and not a four-wheel-drive road, despite a persistent claim to the contrary — the high-clearance warning in circulation belongs to the Iron Gate spur, a different road. Access is from Loomis by Toats Coulee Road, then a Y junction, then NF-39 and NF-300 to the trailhead at about 5,570 ft.

Be careful with the trailhead name. It appears in print as Cathedral Driveway, Chewuch, and Chewack Driveway, and the Chewuch name also belongs to a completely different trailhead near Winthrop. Navigate to the road, not the name.

The Cathedral Driveway descends from its trailhead to join the Chewuch trail #510 around mile 4.8 at about 4,300 ft, and from there it is the Chewuch valley to the Cathedral Lakes basin. Total is about seventeen and a half miles with roughly 3,700 ft of gain — the shortest walk and the least climbing of the three approaches.

The catch is at both ends. The drive is about two hours longer than from Winthrop, and because the trailhead sits high and the trail drops to meet the Chewuch, you finish the trip with roughly 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out, at the point when you least want it.
hazards: About 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out at the end of the trip
Trailhead published under several names; long extra drive
No climbers' trail to the base
Exposed roped climbing; loose, grainy rock on P1 and upper pitches
Hanging belay between P8 and P9 if not linked
Afternoon thunderstorms; remote, with a slow retreat
wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.baseFinding:
The approach changes but the base does not. From camp at Upper Cathedral Lake it is the same thirty to sixty minutes: cross toward the deep gully dividing Cathedral Peak from The Monk, go about 150 feet up into the gully, and start on the left wall from a tall pedestal.

What this approach does affect is your first sighting. Coming down the Chewuch you arrive in the basin from below rather than over Andrews Pass, so take the time at the lake to pick out The Monk as a separate tower leaning against the peak's flank before walking up. The tower in front of the wall is the whole discriminator between this route and the South Face, and it is far easier to identify from across the water than from underneath.

wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.name: Thirtymile Trailhead and the Chewuch River trail toward Remmel Lake

bivy.name: Upper Cathedral Lake basin
bivy.notes: The working climbers' camp for both the Southeast Buttress and Amphitheater's ridges, sitting directly under the peaks with short walks to either. The basin has taken heavy use for decades and the Forest Service has posted revegetation closures on damaged ground here in the past, so treat the shoreline as off limits and camp on rock or bare dirt well back from the water. Check the posted signs on arrival rather than assuming last year's layout still applies — which sites are open has changed between seasons. Nights are cold and exposed at this elevation even in August.
bivy.water: The most dependable water anywhere on this approach — the lake holds through the season and needs no rationing. The one place on the route where you can plan on filling without checking a report first.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at the Andrews Creek trailhead. No quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day fee to park.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites on slabs and benches back from the water; realistically three or four small parties before it feels crowded, and it does fill on midsummer weekends and during larch season

approachLogistics.trailhead: Thirtymile Trailhead (end of the Chewuch River Road)

wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.notes: Follow the Chewuch River trail north from the Thirtymile Trailhead nearly to Remmel Lake, then climb to the Cathedral Lakes basin. A longer way round than Andrews Creek, used when combining the Remmel Lake country with the climb.
hazards: Longest valley approach; trail follows the Chewuch River
No climbers' trail to the base
Exposed roped climbing; loose, grainy rock on P1 and upper pitches
Hanging belay between P8 and P9 if not linked
Afternoon thunderstorms; remote, with a slow retreat

wa_cathedral_peak_southwest_route.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 to Upper Cathedral Lake, then the trail toward Cathedral Pass
wa_cathedral_peak_southwest_route.notes:
Drive north from Winthrop up the Chewuch River road to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,050 ft and walk trail #504 up the drainage to Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft. The lower half is an old burn with no shade and brushy tread. From the pass, drop into the next drainage and take the Cathedral Lakes trail up to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft. That is the base camp and it is a full long day of walking, usually two.

One early-season bonus is worth planning around: the chasm that splits the summit rocks is often snow-filled early, which makes the first step-across easy or trivial. Late season means a bare hole and the pure version of the move. It can snow here in any month, so carry layers whatever the forecast says.

The alternatives are the valley trail from the Thirtymile trailhead, gentle but longer, and the Cathedral Driveway trail from the high trailhead above Loomis (not the longer Iron Gate route), which walks least but drives longest and leaves you 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out.
wa_cathedral_peak_southwest_route.season: July to mid-September; the sunny south-west aspect melts out first
hazards: Old burn on the Andrews Creek trail: no shade, brushy tread; a full long day to Upper Cathedral Lake
Severe fall exposure at the summit chasm step-across; harder descending than ascending; second step-across never has snow
Loose blocks and sandy slopes between Cathedral Pass and the summit; ducks and cairns are the only markers
Snow, verglas or fresh snow possible in any month at 8,600 ft
Lightning on the local high point in afternoon convection
No cell coverage and a 17+ mile evacuation; bears and mosquitoes in the basin
wa_cathedral_peak_southwest_route.baseFinding:
This route has no rock start to find. It begins where you leave the trail, and that spot is defined by the pass, not by a cairn: walk about 0.6 mile of trail from Upper Cathedral Lake toward Cathedral Pass and step off just short of the pass at roughly 7,600 ft. If you have crested the pass and started descending the far side, you have gone too far — turn round.

Above that, the route confirms itself by texture, in a fixed order. First several hundred vertical feet of easy sandy slopes with no rock scrambling at all. Then ducks and cairns over coarse granite blocks and slabs, solid rock, class 2 to 3, with two minor steps that need a hand and one place where a friction push gets you over a block. If you are pulling on anything harder than that, you have wandered off the ducks.

The route then enters a hidden cleft running parallel to and just below the west ridge crest. That cleft is the strongest confirmation on the whole climb, because it cannot be seen from below and you either find yourself in it or you do not.

The last feature is the crux and it is unmistakable: a long chasm cleaving the summit rocks into a north and a south half, with a big chockstone jammed in the slot. Step onto the chockstone and mantle onto the bulge on the far side. The move is easy; the exposure is not, and most parties rig a handline with prusiks for the return. Lower down there is a cannonhole giving an easier alternative to one vertical step.

Negative marker: if at any point you are standing under a thousand-foot wall with a detached tower leaning against its lower right side, you have walked round to the south side of the mountain and you are below the technical routes, not on the walk-up.

wa_cathedral_peak_southwest_route.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee
wa_cathedral_peak_southwest_route.notes: From the Cathedral Driveway Trailhead on the Toats Coulee road out of Loomis, the trail drops to join the Chewuch trail and then climbs the valley to the Cathedral Lakes basin. The eastern way in, with less climbing than Andrews Creek.
hazards: About 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out at the end of the trip
Severe fall exposure at the summit chasm step-across; harder descending
Loose blocks and sandy slopes between Cathedral Pass and the summit; route marked by ducks and cairns only
Snow, verglas or fresh snow possible in any month
Lightning on the local high point in afternoon convection
No cell coverage and a long evacuation; bears and mosquitoes in the basin

wa_cathedral_peak_southwest_route.name: Thirtymile Trailhead and the Chewuch River trail toward Remmel Lake

approachLogistics.trailhead: Thirtymile Trailhead (end of the Chewuch River Road)

wa_cathedral_peak_southwest_route.notes: Follow the Chewuch River trail north from the Thirtymile Trailhead nearly to Remmel Lake, then climb to the Cathedral Lakes basin. A longer way round than Andrews Creek, used when combining the Remmel Lake country with the climb.
hazards: Longer valley walk on the Chewuch trail
Severe fall exposure at the summit chasm step-across; harder descending
Loose blocks and sandy slopes between Cathedral Pass and the summit; route marked by ducks and cairns only
Snow, verglas or fresh snow possible in any month
Lightning on the local high point in afternoon convection
No cell coverage and a long evacuation; bears and mosquitoes in the basin

wa_cathedral_rock_standard.name: Cathedral Pass trail #1345 from the Cle Elum River road end
wa_cathedral_rock_standard.notes:
Drive the Cle Elum River Road, SR 903, to Salmon La Sac, then keep right just past the ranger station onto the rough Forest Road 4330 and follow it about twelve miles to the road end at roughly 3,350 ft.

There are two trailheads within a few yards of each other at the road end and this is the first place to go wrong. The Hyas Lake and Deception Pass trail heads north. You want the Cathedral Rock trail, #1345, heading west, and it may be signed slightly before the road actually ends. Vehicle break-ins have been a recurring problem at this trailhead, which is a pattern rather than a one-off.

The trail reaches Squaw Lake at about two and a half miles and continues to Cathedral Pass at 5,550 ft, roughly four miles in with about 3,400 ft of gain. Turn left, west, onto the Pacific Crest Trail. In less than half a mile you reach the junction with Trail #1375 to Peggy's Pond.

At that junction two climbers' paths head toward the peak, and the counter-intuitive one is the right choice: the left path looks from a distance like the wrong way, but it avoids a scree slope and gives some scrambling instead. Either goes, but do not talk yourself out of the left one on appearances.
wa_cathedral_rock_standard.season: Roughly Jul-Oct. Early season, with the gullies still snow-filled, the rockfall hazard is lower — this is the rare Cascade route that is arguably safer under snow
hazards: Serious rockfall in the summit gully, the peak's named hazard, worst with parties above
Loose rock on the summit scramble as well as in the gully
Picking the Hyas Lake / Deception Pass trailhead by mistake at the road end
Vehicle break-ins at the trailhead
Braided use paths across the meadows near Cathedral Pass
wa_cathedral_rock_standard.baseFinding:
The handrail is elevation plus one named feature. Follow the scramble gully on the right side of the rounded spur upward until the spur runs into the summit formation at about 6,400 ft. That contact point — where broken spur ground ends against continuous rock — is where the approach stops and the climb starts.

From there the line is the obvious gully on the upper left, to the left of the South Buttress. If the buttress is on your left you have gone too far right; the buttress should be to your right as you enter the gully.

One recorded refinement inside that gully, which is around a hundred yards long: stay right at first and cross left higher up, scrambling on rock, rather than taking the centre — the middle holds the loose rock and the steeper steps.

One to two pitches of the southwest face above the gully reach the ridge crest, and most parties rope up for that even though it is graded fourth class. From the crest it is a short scramble to the top.

What is not here, and the absence is worth saying: there is no famous single wrong gully at Cathedral Rock. The published hazard is rockfall and loose rock, stated repeatedly and in plain terms. The genuinely wrong-start stories on this peak are all from the Northeast Buttress, a different route on the other side, so do not import them.

wa_cathedral_rock_standard.name: Peggy's Pond, gaining the summit gully from the ledge above the pond
wa_cathedral_rock_standard.notes:
Walk to Cathedral Pass as for the standard, then continue on Trail #1375 to Peggy's Pond. The final half mile or so into the pond is primitive, crossing narrow ledges with real exposure, and it feels harder than anything on the maintained trail before it.

Peggy's Pond is the last reliable water and the last established camp, so this is the variant for parties splitting the day or combining the climb with Mount Daniel.
wa_cathedral_rock_standard.season: Same window; the ledge traverse into the pond is nastier with a heavy pack or under snow
hazards: Exposed narrow ledge traverse on the way into Peggy's Pond
Rockfall in the summit gully
Snow lingering on the pond ledges into early summer
wa_cathedral_rock_standard.baseFinding:
From the pond you gain the same summit gully, but from below and on the south side rather than by traversing in from the pass. Climb to the ledge above the pond and follow it to the foot of the gully system.

The identification is unchanged: you want the gully to the left of the South Buttress, entered where the spur ground dies against the continuous summit rock near 6,400 ft. Coming from the pond you meet that rock from underneath, so the check is that the buttress stands to your right as you turn up into the gully.

wa_chair_peak_northeast_buttress.name: Source Lake basin to the divide (summer and fall rock)
wa_chair_peak_northeast_buttress.notes: Upper Alpental lot, I-90 exit 52. Snow Lake Trail up the valley — the first stretch is the old ski-area cat track — to the fork at about 1.5 miles, then left/west toward Source Lake, where the maintained trail ends near 3,700-3,740 ft. Leave the tread and head northwest into the basin below Chair's east face on climbers' path, talus and heather. The Thumb Tack, a freestanding rock in the basin, is the landmark to aim for; parties commonly reach it in about two hours from the car. At the Thumb Tack there is a genuine fork in what you do next. Continuing up the basin takes you to the foot of the east face. For the Northeast Buttress, angle sharply right from the Thumb Tack and scramble rocky heather slopes and ledges to the top of the divide, then walk along the north side of the divide to the base of the buttress. That line is less obvious than the gully but easier and less exposed.
hazards: loose rock on the heather-and-ledge scramble up to the divide
the basin sits under avalanche terrain off Chair Peak and Snoqualmie Mountain
rockfall onto the gully from parties above
no water above the Source Lake outlet
wa_chair_peak_northeast_buttress.baseFinding:
The start is unmistakable once you have it in view, and every route description carries a photo of it: a blocky S-shaped gully, sometimes described as an open book, beginning just down and right of the divide. It climbs, curves right, then straightens again and finishes in a clump of trees. Two pitches of gully and chimney.

The clump of trees at the top of the S is the confirmation. If the gully in front of you runs straight with no rightward curve, and nothing green at its top, it is not the route.

In poor visibility, take the Thumb Tack as your last certain position and navigate from there: sharply right and up to the divide, then everything else happens on the divide's north side. If you are on the south or east side of the divide looking at the east face, you have not crossed over yet.

Above the gully the buttress continues on blocky low-angle rock, angling left across exposed slabby ledges toward another cluster of trees near the prow.

wa_chair_peak_northeast_buttress.name: Winter and spring, on snow
wa_chair_peak_northeast_buttress.notes: Same line up the valley, but in snow the summer tread is abandoned and parties skin or boot the valley bottom to Source Lake, then up into the basin, commonly reaching the Thumb Tack shortly after first light. Skis are cached in the basin. In snow the approach gully from the basin up toward the buttress is itself the hazard: it is a classic early-season slide path, and trip reports from this basin describe deep postholing, wet-slab activity and wind loading. Rope, axe and crampons usually come out from the basin onward rather than at the base of the route, because the approach gully is exposed enough on its own.
hazards: the approach gully to the buttress is a known early-season slide path
wind loading and wet-slab activity reported repeatedly in this basin
deep postholing on the basin approach
avalanche terrain the length of the Alpental valley below
wa_chair_peak_northeast_buttress.baseFinding:
Same S-shaped gully, curving right and finishing in trees. Under snow the curve is easier to read from a distance than close up, so pick the line out from the basin before you commit to the divide, and hold that picture.

The trees at the top of the S are what stay visible when the rock is plastered. If you are at the foot of a straight snow runnel with no trees above it, you are on a different feature.

If the ground you are on is exposed and you have not yet crossed to the north side of the divide, stop — the gully line direct to the ridge is steeper and more exposed than the walk along the divide's north side, and it is not the recommended way to the base.

wa_chikamin_peak_southeast_slopes.name: PCT from Snoqualmie Pass, leaving the trail half a mile short of Chikamin Pass
camps: Ridge Lake and Gravel Lake, PCT beyond Kendall Katwalk
Ridge Lake / Gravel Lake saddle camps
wa_chikamin_peak_southeast_slopes.notes:
From the PCT North trailhead, Trail #2000, off I-90 exit 52, the trail switchbacks through timber and avalanche paths, crosses beneath Kendall Peak, and reaches the Kendall Katwalk around mile 5 at about 5,400 ft — a good checkpoint, though not reliable water late in the season.

Continue north past Ridge Lake at about mile 6.5, which has reliable camping and water, and the Alaska Lake and Joe Lake junctions, then along the rolling rocky PCT beneath Alaska and Huckleberry Mountains to the Huckleberry-Chikamin saddle around mile 10.25. The trail then contours below the Four Brothers and Chikamin's south face, passing the Park Lakes Trail junction.

About 13.5 miles one way to the base of the gullies with roughly 4,600 ft of gain, so most parties camp at Ridge Lake or the pack camp near the turnoff and make it a two or three day trip.
hazards: Long trail approach (about 13.5 miles one way) with camps well short of the peak
Unmarked gully turnoff half a mile short of Chikamin Pass; overshooting puts you among the cliffy Four Brothers
Loose scree and rockfall in the upper gully system
Steep snow-filled, rubble-choked gully in early season
Short but exposed Class 3 moves on the summit horn
wa_chikamin_peak_southeast_slopes.baseFinding:
The test is to leave the trail before you reach the pass, and that is counter-intuitive enough that it is the whole finding. At roughly mile 13.5 — about half a mile short of Chikamin Pass, near an established pack camp where the trail dips to about 5,500 ft — leave the PCT and climb steep grassy and heather slopes into the gully systems on the south and southeast face.

The negative is explicit and expensive: do not continue to Chikamin Pass before cutting uphill. Doing so puts you in the middle of the Four Brothers, a band of cliffy towers that force technical terrain on a route that is otherwise a scramble. If you are standing at Chikamin Pass, you have overshot the turn.

So use the pack camp as the marker: an established camp on the trail, with the peak's south face above and the pass still ahead of you. Turn uphill there.

What the ground should do, in order: class 2 hiking low on grass and heather, then loose scree and dirt-and-heather slots in the upper gully, sustained class 3 as you gain Chikamin Ridge with some exposure near the crest, and finally a short, well-protected class 3-4 chimney or slot of about 10 ft right below the summit block, with roughly 75 more feet of easy scrambling above it to the top. A 10 ft chimney immediately below the summit horn is the confirming feature.

Snow changes the character of the gully entirely: early in the season it is a steep, rubble-choked chute and an axe is needed.

wa_chikamin_peak_southeast_slopes.name: Mineral Creek and Park Lakes, then the gullies above Glacier Lake

bivy.name: Park Lakes basin
bivy.notes: The standard camp for Chikamin Peak's southeast slopes, and the reason Chikamin is the peak in this group least honestly described as a Snoqualmie Pass objective. Most parties reach it from Mineral Creek on the far eastern side, walking up from a trailhead at around 2,375 ft — an approach that begins nowhere near I-90 exit 52. From the pass it is reachable instead by the PCT north over Chikamin Pass, which is a long day in itself. Upper Park Lake sits at about 4,700 ft in open meadow and rolling ground with roomy sites, and a short side trail drops around 550 ft to Glacier Lake where there are more sites on the north shore among boulders and heather. From the basin the southeast slopes rise directly toward the summit. Note the campfire ban is specific to this basin rather than an elevation rule, and it is enforced — the meadows are fragile and the ground here recovers slowly.
bivy.water: The lakes and the basin outlets run all season. Treat it.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at whichever trailhead you start from. Campfires are prohibited in the Park Lakes basin outright, and above 5,000 ft generally on this side of the crest. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. The eastern approaches were inside the 2026 wildfire closure area; confirm before driving out.
bivy.capacity: Large established sites among trees and meadow at Upper Park Lake, comfortable for a group; more sites at Glacier Lake below

approachLogistics.trailhead: Mineral Creek Trailhead (Trail #1331, end of FR-46)

wa_chikamin_peak_southeast_slopes.notes:
From the Mineral Creek trailhead, Trail #1331, at the end of FR-46 / Cooper Pass Road at about 2,400 ft, the trail is brushy low down but well trodden. It climbs steadily beside Mineral Creek to Park Lakes at 4.3 to 5.4 miles and about 2,570 ft of gain, and ties into the PCT.

From the PCT / Park Lakes junction, head north toward the Spectacle Point saddle overlooking Spectacle Lake, then drop about a mile to Glacier Lake, a common camp, before climbing the southeast-slope gullies above it.

This is the shortest line in — day-trip feasible for a strong party at roughly 14 to 16.5 miles round trip — but the tread is rougher and there are creek crossings low down.
hazards: Brushy lower trail and creek crossings on the Mineral Creek approach, no maintained tread
Loose scree and rockfall in the upper gullies above Glacier Lake
Snow-filled gullies in early season
Exposure near the final ridge crest; short exposed Class 3 moves on the summit horn
wa_chikamin_peak_southeast_slopes.baseFinding:
From this side the arrival is a lake, not a trail junction: you climb the gullies directly above Glacier Lake. Standing at the lake with the southeast slopes rising in front of you is the arrival, and the lake is a hard landmark that cloud does not remove.

What the ground below the gullies looks like, as confirmation: brooks, waterfalls, tarns, heather benches, sandstone slabs and blocky breccia low down. Running water and heather benches are right for this side; if you are on bare scree from the lake upward, you have started too high.

The two approaches meet on the same upper mountain, so the finding from there is identical: loose scree and dirt-and-heather slots in the upper gully, sustained class 3 to the crest of Chikamin Ridge, and a short well-protected 10 ft class 3-4 chimney below the summit block with about 75 ft of easy scrambling above it.

And the same negative applies once you are on the PCT: do not wander south toward Chikamin Pass looking for a way up. The Four Brothers sit between the pass and the route.

wa_chiwawa_mountain_southwest.name: Trinity and the Chiwawa River Trail to Chiwawa Basin and the 6,300 ft benches
wa_chiwawa_mountain_southwest.notes:
Park at Trinity Trailhead near 2,800 ft at the end of Chiwawa River Road/FR-6200 by the old mine site. Start up-valley on Buck Creek Trail #1513 for about a mile and a half and bear right at the fork onto Chiwawa River Trail #1550, which takes over an old mining-road grade close to the river — water is reliable along all of this.

About 3.7 more miles brings the signed Red Mountain Trail junction near 4,000 ft. This is the last water that is both obvious and easy to reach before the basin, so fill here. Bear left into Chiwawa Basin rather than taking the right-hand switchbacks up Red Mountain.

Beyond the junction the tread deteriorates, braids and climbs through forest toward the basin, with an unbridged ford of the Chiwawa headwater around 4,400 ft — manageable at summer flow, higher and pushier early. Above the ford the brush thickens and the tread fades: favour the more open, less-timbered ground along the east side of the basin, because drifting into the timber turns this into a bushwhack.

Camp is on benches around 6,300 ft. Several lines reach them: the left-trending gully is the most direct and easiest going though it is wet, and the vegetated slopes beside the talus gullies are the better choice coming down.

FR-6200 has been closed to vehicles beyond Atkinson Flat since May 20, 2026 under storm-damage order 06-17-07-2026-11 (through December 31, 2027), so Trinity is not reachable by vehicle. The Little Giant Fire closure (order 06-17-07-2026-40) also closes the Chiwawa River Road and the trails from Trinity through October 31, 2026 unless lifted sooner.
wa_chiwawa_mountain_southwest.season: Late Jun-Sep. The road to Trinity is often not melted out until mid-June, and the upper mountain and col hold snow into July in heavy years
hazards: Misidentifying the gully near the col, which leads to an exposed low-fifth-class dead end
Loose, sandy rock flanking the col and loose talus on the upper mountain
Cornices and early-season snow at the Fortress-Chiwawa col
An unbridged ford of the Chiwawa headwater, and fading braided tread that becomes a bushwhack if you drift into timber
FR-6200 closed beyond Atkinson Flat since May 20, 2026 (order 06-17-07-2026-11, through December 31, 2027), so Trinity is unreachable by vehicle
wa_chiwawa_mountain_southwest.baseFinding:
The base is a notch in somebody else's ridge, and saying it that way is what makes it findable: the Fortress-Chiwawa col at about 7,200 ft is the notch in Fortress Mountain's east ridge. From the 6,300 ft benches, traverse steep heather and aim for that notch. You are walking toward a gap on the skyline of the mountain next door, not toward the peak you are climbing.

What the last stretch feels like, so you know you are on it: the snow slope up to the col is moderate and then steepens noticeably in the final section below the notch, and the rock flanking it is loose and sandy. Stay on the snow or on the most solid line you can find rather than the flanking rock. A slope that stays uniformly moderate all the way to a gap is not this one.

From the col the route has no single line and that is the correct answer, not a gap in the beta: work up the south-west side on slabs, gullies and talus taking the path of least resistance. Nothing here is cairned or named.

The negative marker is explicit and it has a stated consequence: misidentifying the correct gully near the col leads to an exposed low-fifth-class dead end. If the ground you are on has stopped offering an easy option and is committing you to fifth-class moves, reverse and pick a different line — this route never needs them.

The crux is short and it is at the top: the step gaining the summit ridge is loose and exposed Class 2-3 and is the hardest ground on the route. After it, an easy traverse of about 100 ft to the west — to your right — reaches the top. If you gain a ridge and the summit is to your left, you are on the wrong section of crest.

Going back down, use a different line than you came up for one stretch only: below the benches, the vegetated slopes beside the talus gullies are the better descent, and the loose climber's-left skyline gully should be avoided.

wa_chiwawa_mountain_southwest.name: Phelps Creek variant to the col west of the summit
wa_chiwawa_mountain_southwest.notes:
A less-travelled alternative starts at the Phelps Creek Trailhead rather than Trinity. It bushwhacks to about 5,500 ft and follows a gully to the right of Point 5971 up to the col west of the summit, then takes easy Class 2 ground along the west ridge to the top.

This is the shorter line on paper and the rougher one on the ground: there is no tread on the bushwhack and no camp equivalent to the Chiwawa Basin benches. It is genuinely used, but not recommended over the Trinity approach.
wa_chiwawa_mountain_southwest.season: Late Jun-Sep, as for the main line
hazards: An unmaintained bushwhack with no tread from about 5,500 ft and no published landmarks below the gully
No established camp on this side, so it commits you to a long day
Early-season snow in the gully and at the col
Loose rock on the west ridge, as everywhere on this peak
wa_chiwawa_mountain_southwest.baseFinding:
This variant's base is a different col from the main route's, and confusing the two puts you on the wrong side of the mountain. The standard line goes to the Fortress-Chiwawa col, which is south-west of the summit and is a notch in Fortress's east ridge. This variant goes to the col west of the summit, gained from Phelps Creek by a gully to the right of Point 5971.

The test is what lies above the col you reach. From this one, the West Ridge runs to the summit on easy Class 2 ground — a walk, essentially. From the Fortress-Chiwawa col you face slabs, gullies and talus on the south-west face with a loose Class 2-3 step at the top. If you have reached a col and the way on is a broad easy crest, you are on this variant. If it is a face with no obvious line, you are on the standard one.

The approach marker is a numbered point and that is all there is: the gully is to the right of Point 5971. Nothing else about the bushwhack below it is published, which is why this is the second variant and not the first. Carry a track.

wa_clark_mountain_west_ridge.name: Boulder Creek and the sheepherder's trail to the south basin — the non-glacier line
wa_clark_mountain_west_ridge.notes: Start at the White River trailhead at the end of White River Road, FR 6400, at about 2,300 ft; a Northwest Forest Pass is needed. Walk the White River trail #1507 about four flat miles — one party gained all of three hundred feet in a little over an hour — to the Boulder Creek trail #1562 junction. Turn east up Boulder Creek. At about the 5,000 ft level, roughly four and a half miles up this trail, pick up an old sheepherder's trail heading west and follow it to around 5,600 to 5,700 ft. Note that published mileages on this stretch do not reconcile cleanly between sources, so navigate by elevation and by the basin rather than by a mile count. There is a faint path that contours, crosses the creek and climbs the west side of Boulder Creek, firming up into decent tread as it gains the slope. Leave the sheepherder's trail in the basin above Boulder Creek around 5,700 ft and climb open heather north-north-west to the southern ridge running off Clark's south-east peak, Point 8373. Car to summit is given as about eleven and a half miles one way with roughly 6,500 ft of gain, and essentially every party camps in the Boulder Creek basin rather than trying it in a day.
hazards: Getting cliffed out on the spur while looking for a gully that is really a ledge
Unbridged Boulder Creek crossing, cold and thigh-deep early season and sometimes braided
Losing the sheepherder's trail — it is notoriously hard to find from the White River trail

wa_clark_mountain_west_ridge.baseFinding: Everything turns on one feature and it is misdescribed by its own name. Published descriptions call it the one and only easy gully breaching the ridge — the way down off the spur into Clark's south basin — and it leaves the crest at about 7,200 to 7,300 ft. The correction, from a climber who found it: it is Class 2, and it feels more like a sloping ledge than a gully. Parties hunting for a defined cleft walk past it and get cliffed out. Two accounts both put it at 7,200 ft and both anchor it to the south spur of Point 8373, so the elevation is the reliable half of the identification and the word gully is the unreliable half. The positional cue that puts you in the right place to look: there is a flattish section of the spur at 7,200 ft that is reached easily on scree and grass. Stand on that flat and you can see the south slope of Clark, which looks easy — and it is. The difficulty is purely in getting down to it, which is what the ledge is for. Drop a couple of hundred feet down that ledge, then contour the upper south basin on broken rock and patches of permanent snow to the final south ridge and a short Class 3 scramble to the top. A note on names before you cross-reference anything: the Walrus Glacier is shown as the Clark Glacier on maps. They are one feature with two names.

wa_clark_mountain_west_ridge.name: Boulder Pass and the Walrus Glacier — the glacier line
wa_clark_mountain_west_ridge.notes:
Approach identically to Boulder Basin: White River trail #1507 four miles to the Boulder Creek trail #1562, then up into the open basin at roughly 5,300 ft, about five to six hours and three thousand feet from the car. That basin is the camp.

From camp, climb north-east to Boulder Pass at about 6,300 to 6,330 ft. Drop down steep snow on the far side, then climb to a bench at about 6,700 ft on Clark's eastern arm.

The bench is where you rope up. Do it there, before you go anywhere, because of what comes next.
wa_clark_mountain_west_ridge.season: Roughly late Jun-Sep, on the earlier side while the crevasses are still bridged
hazards: Crevasses and snowbridges on the lower Walrus Glacier
Steep snow on the far side of Boulder Pass
No view of the glacier until you have committed around the eastern arm
Unbridged Boulder Creek ford lower down
The 7,200 ft south-basin gully is a landmark for a different route and will mislead you here
wa_clark_mountain_west_ridge.baseFinding:
You cannot see the Walrus Glacier until you are committed to it. From the 6,700 ft bench you wrap around Clark's eastern arm, and only then does the glacier come into view for the first time. That is why the bench is the roping-up point rather than the glacier's edge — there is no convenient stopping place once you are round the corner.

The entry is specific and it is not the middle of the toe: go up a moderately steep chute on the left, southern margin of the glacier. Expect to step over several narrow crevasses and, in at least one recorded year, to cross a snowbridge over a large one.

Once on the gentle upper glacier the summit wedge is visible in the distance and the navigation problem is over. The finish skirts the upper south face of that wedge on a steep snowfield and ends with a short scramble onto the summit rocks — about six hours from camp.

Negative marker, and this one matters because it would send you to the wrong landmark entirely: the famous one-and-only-easy-gully at 7,200 ft belongs to the south basin route, not to this one. If you are on the Walrus you never touch it. A published page titled for the Walrus Glacier in fact describes the south-basin line in its turn-by-turn, so read carefully which route a description is actually walking.

wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.name: Phelps Creek and Spider Gap (standard)
camps: Phelps Creek Campground and the Chiwawa River road campgrounds
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.notes: From the Phelps Creek Trailhead (~3,500 ft), Trail #1511 climbs the valley about 6.5 miles to Spider Meadows, then into upper Phelps Basin and up the Spider Glacier snowfield to Spider Gap at 7,100 ft. Descend the north side — the steepest 100 vertical feet first, softer snow tends to be climber's-left — then scree and easing snowfield past the Lyman Glacier to Lower Lyman Lake, and back up about 1.8 miles of open meadow to Cloudy Pass at 6,438 ft. This is the line the recorded distance matches.
hazards: Spider Gap: permanent snow slope that can hold open crevasses and firm icy snow early season; axe and crampons

Exposed, unprotected Class 3-4 summit block with steep drop-off
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.baseFinding: Cloudy Pass is the staging point, not the base: the climbing starts where the boot path leaves the meadows and gains the southwest ridge, with the summit about 1,500 ft above the pass.

wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.name: Buck Creek Trail from Trinity, over Buck Creek Pass

bivy.name: Lyman Lakes and Cloudy Pass
bivy.notes: This basin is the reason North Star Mountain, Cloudy Peak and Chiwawa Mountain sit in the same zone as Bonanza — it is reachable from both sides and belongs to neither. From the west it is roughly two miles and 1,700 ft above Spider Meadow over Spider Gap, crossing the permanent snowfield below the gap and dropping onto the Lyman Glacier, which puts an ice axe and traction on the packing list even in August. From the east it is a long valley walk up Railroad Creek from Holden, with intermediate camps at Hart Lake and at Rebel Camp about a mile beyond it that break the approach in two. North Star and Cloudy are scrambles off the Cloudy Pass trail from here; Chiwawa is reached by traversing the Lyman Glacier to its east ridge, which is a roped glacier objective rather than a walk. Cloudy Pass itself is scenic and thoroughly exposed to wind and lightning. With the Holden road closed and the Chiwawa road under its own closures, both ends of this corridor have been unreachable at times through 2026.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lakes, the Lyman Glacier outflow and creeks all through the basin
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit. Camping and campfires are prohibited within 200 feet of Lyman Lake's shoreline, so pitch back from the water; carry a stove rather than planning on a fire. Reached from the west, no recreation pass is needed at the Phelps Creek trailhead, which the Forest Service lists as a no-fee site; reached from the east it needs the ferry and bus booking instead.
bivy.capacity: Established sites at Lower Lyman Lake, more scattered ground toward the upper lakes, and a small number of exposed camps at Cloudy Pass; a popular corridor, so plan on sharing
